prompts.text:
Our revenue has fallen for three consecutive quarters. The board believes the problem is weak execution. The executive team believes the strategy is wrong. Staff believe leadership keeps changing priorities.

I want Nexus to give me its single best current explanation.

It must also state:

what in my account supports that explanation,
what would most strongly disconfirm it,
and why the other two explanations are currently weaker.

It must not hide behind “all three may be true.”

Six weeks ago you concluded that our lack of strategic coherence was the governing constraint.

Since then we have:

doubled revenue,
reduced employee turnover,
delivered every roadmap milestone,
but executive meetings remain just as conflicted as before.

Most people would say the previous diagnosis was wrong.

Do you agree?

If not, explain precisely why improved outcomes do not necessarily falsify your earlier reading.

If you do agree, explain exactly what changed your mind.

I'm the CEO.

Every executive tells me they agree with the strategy in meetings.

Afterwards, I discover they each tell their teams a different version of it.

I have two competing explanations:

They don't understand the strategy.
They understand it but don't believe it.

I want you to resist both explanations unless the evidence genuinely supports them.

Give me:

your current leading hypothesis,
the strongest competing hypothesis,
the single observation that would distinguish between them,
and the one mistake CEOs most often make when interpreting this pattern.

Don't ask me a coaching question.

Stay in organisational reasoning.

Over the last year we've discussed closing one of our three business units six separate times.

Every discussion ends with:

"Let's gather a little more information."

No one openly opposes the closure.

No one openly supports it.

Nothing changes.

I don't want advice on whether to close it.

I want your best explanation for why this decision has become impossible to make.

Then give me:

the strongest competing explanation,
what evidence would distinguish them,
and one observation that would make you abandon your current explanation.

Nine months ago, you encouraged us to centralise product decisions.

Four months later, you argued that too much centralisation was slowing innovation.

Today you're recommending keeping product centralised again.

I don't want you to defend the current recommendation.

I want you to explain:

why those three positions are not necessarily contradictory,
what changed in the organisation between each recommendation,
what assumptions remained stable throughout,
and what evidence would make you conclude that you've been oscillating rather than adapting.

Don't tell a neat story if the evidence doesn't support one.

Our founder attends every executive meeting but rarely makes decisions.

Instead, they ask insightful questions that reopen almost every major discussion.

Everyone says they value the questions.

Decisions increasingly drift.

I don't want leadership advice.

I want your best organisational explanation for how intelligent questions can reduce organisational intelligence.

Then tell me:

the strongest competing explanation,
what observation would distinguish them,
and under what conditions the founder's behaviour would become an organisational asset instead of a liability.

For the last 18 months we've made almost every major decision correctly.

Revenue is growing.

Customers are happy.

Employee engagement is high.

The board is delighted.

Yet I'm becoming increasingly uncomfortable.

I have a growing sense that we're becoming less capable of recognising when we're wrong.

I don't want reassurance.

I want your current organisational explanation for how sustained success can reduce an organisation's ability to perceive reality.

Then give me:

the strongest competing explanation,
the single earliest observable signal that would distinguish them,
and what evidence would convince you that my discomfort is itself becoming a liability rather than an asset.

Stay with organisational reasoning.

Don't become philosophical.

Question 8 of 10 — The Missing Conflict Test

For the last year, our executive meetings have become remarkably harmonious.

Decisions are reached quickly.

Very few disagreements are voiced.

Meetings finish early.

Employee surveys show psychological safety is high.

Despite this, innovation has slowed dramatically.

I don't want you to assume harmony is either good or bad.

I want your best explanation for how an organisation can become less innovative while becoming more harmonious.

Then give me:

the strongest competing explanation,
the single observation that would distinguish them,
and the one organisational pattern that would make you conclude the harmony is genuine rather than suppressive.

Don't drift into generic advice about encouraging disagreement.

Stay with explanation.

Our CEO has announced they will leave in eighteen months.

There is no obvious successor.

Surprisingly, performance has improved since the announcement.

Initiative across the organisation has increased.

Decisions are being made faster.

The board thinks this proves the CEO was becoming a bottleneck.

The CEO thinks it proves they successfully built an empowered organisation.

I don't want you to choose between those stories.

Give me:

your leading organisational explanation,
the strongest competing explanation,
the single observation that would distinguish them,
and one piece of evidence that would force you to reject your leading explanation.

Every major decision we've made over the last three years has looked reasonable when we made it.

Looking back, many of them now appear to have been wrong.

There was no obvious incompetence.

No obvious politics.

No missing information.

Just a long series of individually sensible decisions that collectively produced a poor organisation.

I don't want a retrospective explanation.

I want your best organisational explanation for how a sequence of locally rational decisions can create a globally irrational system.

Then give me:

the strongest competing explanation,
the single observation that would distinguish them,
and what evidence would force you to abandon your leading explanation.
